mainTopic: Paying for living in another's חצר without permission, and an animal eating produce at the edge of the public square
overview: This amud opens by finishing an answer about הקדש: using הקדש always counts as if the Owner knew. Then רבי אבא בר זבדא sends a question to רב הונא: must someone who lives in another person's חצר without permission pay rent? רב הונא dies before answering. His son reports, in the name of רב, that no rent is owed. He also reports that a person who unknowingly rented a house that belonged to someone else must pay that real owner. The גמרא explains that the difference is whether the place is normally rented out, and a second report says the same. רב gives a reason from a פסוק (an empty house falls to ruin), and רב יוסף gives a similar reason. The story of רב נחמן and the orphans' land is shown not to disagree, because the orphans lost real income. Next the גמרא turns to the משנה about an animal eating food in the public square. רב and שמואל argue, in several versions, about an animal that turns its head, and about space a person gives over to public use. The amud ends as the גמרא begins rejecting a suggestion that this argument depends on the law of a בור dug in one's own property; the rejection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Using הקדש is like using a regular person's property with his knowledge
steps.stepSummary: The last words of an earlier rejection. A proof from מעילה does not work, because using הקדש counts as if the owner knew.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is treated like an ordinary person's property used with his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer begun on the previous daf. It explains why a proof from the laws of הקדש does not prove anything about living in a friend's חצר without his knowledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With הקדש, the Owner is ה׳, who always knows. So using הקדש is never really 'without the owner knowing.' That means the rule that one is liable for מעילה cannot teach us about a person who lives in a חצר without the owner's knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary person, as opposed to הקדש
With knowledge or awareness
It is similar to, it is treated like

phrases.english: Is similar to an ordinary person's property used with his knowledge.
phrases.notes: This wraps up an answer from the previous daf: using הקדש is never 'without the Owner knowing.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the rejection of a proof from הקדש that began on the previous daf.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from מעילה about using another person's property without his knowledge.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: With הקדש the Owner always knows, so it is not a true case of 'without his knowledge.'

steps.title: A question sent to רב הונא about living in a friend's חצר
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר זבדא asks מרי בר מר to put a question to רב הונא: must someone who lives in another's חצר without his knowledge pay rent? רב הונא dies before he can answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא sent a message to מרי בר מר: Ask רב הונא whether a person who lives in his friend's חצר without his knowledge must pay him rent. Meanwhile, רב הונא passed away.
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is asked: does a person who lived in someone else's property without permission owe rent? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the owner can demand payment when the user benefited but did not ask. The question goes unanswered because רב הונא died, so the answer will have to come from someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Another person's courtyard or property
To pay him rent
Meanwhile, in the meantime
He passed away (literally, his soul rested)

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent a message
to Mari bar Mar:
Ask this question of Rav Huna:
phrases.notes: מרי בר מר is being asked to bring the question to רב הונא.

phrases.english: One who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge,

phrases.aramaic: צָרִיךְ לְהַעֲלוֹת לוֹ שָׂכָר, אוֹ לָא?
phrases.english: must he pay him rent, or not?
Meanwhile, Rav Huna passed away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the main question again, now sent to a specific אמורא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether someone who lives in another's חצר without permission must pay rent.

steps.title: רבה בר רב הונא reports two rulings in the name of רב
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא answers in his father's name, quoting רב: no rent is owed. He also reports a second ruling: one who rents a house from ראובן pays rent to שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: This is what my father, my master, said in the name of רב: He does not need to pay him rent. And one who rents a house from ראובן pays rent to שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The son of רב הונא gives the answer his father would have given: the person who lived there does not have to pay. He also adds a second, puzzling ruling about ראובן and שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ruling answers the question directly: no rent is owed. The second ruling is said in a short, unclear way, so the גמרא will need to explain it next.

keyTerms.meaning: My father, my master (here, רב הונא)
In the name of רב
One who rents

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי אָמַר אַבָּא מָרִי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: So said my father, my master, in the name of Rav:
He does not need to pay him rent.
And one who rents a house from Reuven
pays rent to Shimon.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אָמַר אַבָּא מָרִי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question that רב הונא could not answer himself.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No rent is owed. A second ruling is added: renting from ראובן means paying שמעון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who lives in another's חצר without his knowledge does not pay rent.

steps.title: What does שמעון have to do with it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is confused by the second ruling: why would the renter pay שמעון if he rented from ראובן?
steps.simpleTranslation: What does שמעון have to do with this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about the wording of the second ruling. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter made his deal with ראובן, so paying שמעון makes no sense at first. The גמרא needs to know what case is being described.

keyTerms.meaning: What is his business here? What does he have to do with it?

phrases.english: Shimon, what does he have to do with this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the unclear wording of the second ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What case the ruling about ראובן and שמעון is describing.

steps.title: The house turned out to belong to שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The ruling means the house turned out to belong to שמעון, not ראובן, so the renter pays שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he means: if the house turns out to belong to שמעון, the renter pays rent to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second ruling. The renter thought he rented from ראובן, but the real owner was שמעון, so he must pay שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the case is clear: the renter actually lived in שמעון's house without שמעון knowing. Yet he still has to pay rent, which seems to clash with the first ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he means
It turned out, it was discovered

phrases.english: This is what he is saying:
If the house turns out to be Shimon's,
he pays him rent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what שמעון has to do with the case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The house really belonged to שמעון, so the renter must pay him.

steps.title: The two rulings seem to contradict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the same source can say both 'no rent' and 'pay rent to שמעון.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Two opposite rulings?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a clash between the two rulings it just heard. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases someone lived in another person's property without the owner knowing. The first ruling says no rent is owed, but the שמעון ruling says rent is owed.

keyTerms.meaning: Two (here: two rulings that clash)

phrases.english: Two contradictory rulings?!
phrases.notes: The first ruling said no rent, but the שמעון ruling said pay rent, and both are 'without the owner knowing.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two rulings that were just explained.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two rulings reported in the name of רב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both cases involve living in another's property without his knowledge, yet one ruling says no rent and the other says rent.

steps.title: It depends on whether the place is usually rented out
steps.stepSummary: The rulings deal with different kinds of property. If the place is normally rented out, rent is owed. If it is not, no rent is owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ruling is about a place that is normally rented out; that ruling is about a place that is not normally rented out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by splitting the cases. The שמעון house is one that is usually rented, so rent is owed. The first ruling is about a place that is not usually rented.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a property is normally rented, the owner actually lost money because he could have rented it out. When it is not normally rented, the owner lost nothing, so the user does not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: This case... that case (used to split two cases)
Stands to be rented out, is normally rented

steps.whatToRemember: No rent is owed for living in someone's חצר without permission if it is not normally rented out. If it is normally rented out, like the house of שמעון, rent must be paid.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the person never owes rent. The ruling of no rent applies only when the place was not going to be rented anyway.
steps.whyThisMatters: This split between property that is or is not normally rented becomes the key line for the rest of the sugya about benefiting from someone else's property.

phrases.english: This is where it stands to be rented out,
phrases.notes: This first 'הא' is the שמעון ruling, where rent is owed.

phrases.english: that is where it does not stand to be rented out.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא דְּקָיְימָא לְאַגְרָא הָא דְּלָא קָיְימָא לְאַגְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ruling refers to a different type of property.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two rulings seemed to be about the same situation and so contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Rent is owed only for property that is normally rented out. No rent is owed for property that is not.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether rent is owed depends on whether the owner normally rents out the property.

steps.title: A second report of the same ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another report, from רבי חייא בר אבין, of the two rulings. Some trace it to רב and some to רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught: someone living in his friend's courtyard without the friend knowing does not have to pay rent. But someone who rents a house from the townspeople must pay rent to the owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up what רבה בר רב הונא reported by showing that another חכם said the same two rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording here is a little different. Instead of 'renting from ראובן and paying שמעון,' it says renting 'from the townspeople' and paying 'the owners.' That new wording is about to cause a question.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated: another report that supports what was just said
And some say it: a second version of who said the teaching
The townspeople, meaning the house seemed to be public property
To pay rent

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin said that Rav said,
and some say it this way:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin said that Rav Huna said:
One who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge
does not need to pay him rent,
and one who rents a house from the townspeople
pays rent to the owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a parallel report that supports the rulings from step 3
steps.raayaObject: רבה בר רב הונא's report of the two rulings
steps.raayaSupportSource: An independent report from רבי חייא בר אבין, in the name of רב or רב הונא

steps.title: Who are these owners?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'owners' have to do with a house rented from the townspeople.
steps.simpleTranslation: Owners? What do they have to do with this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is confused by the word 'owners.' The renter dealt with the town, so who are these owners?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the renter paid the town, it seems no private owner is involved at all. So why would rent go to someone called 'the owners'?

keyTerms.meaning: Owners
What do they have to do with it?

phrases.english: Owners, what do they have to do with this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a word in the ruling just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How private owners fit into a case of renting from the town

steps.title: The house turned out to have owners
steps.stepSummary: It means the house was later found to belong to private owners, so the renter pays them.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he meant: if it turns out the house had owners, the renter pays rent to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the house seemed to be public, but it turned out to belong to someone. That owner gets the rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same idea as step 5, just in this version's words. The renter planned to pay rent, so he pays it to the real owner.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he meant
It turned out to have owners

phrases.english: This is what he is saying:
if it turns out it had owners,
rent is paid to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the owners
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The house was thought to be public but turned out to be privately owned, so the owners get the rent

steps.title: Two rulings that seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how one source can say both 'no rent' and 'pay rent.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Two rulings that contradict each other?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two rulings seem to clash, just as it did in step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases someone used another person's property. Yet one ruling says no rent and the other says pay rent.

keyTerms.meaning: Two, meaning two rulings that seem to contradict

phrases.english: Two contradictory rulings?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the two rulings now that both are clear
steps.kashyaTarget: The two rulings in the report of רבי חייא בר אבין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both cases involve using someone else's property, so they should get the same ruling

steps.title: Property for rent versus property not for rent
steps.stepSummary: Rent is owed for a place usually rented out. No rent is owed for a place that is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one is a place that is usually rented out. That one is a place that is not usually rented out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash by saying the two rulings talk about different kinds of property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner normally rents the place out, the person living there cost him money, so he must pay. If the owner would not have rented it anyway, he lost nothing, so no rent is owed.

keyTerms.meaning: Normally stands to be rented out
This one, that one: splitting two rulings into two cases

steps.whatToRemember: The ruling depends on whether the owner lost anything. Pay for a place that is normally rented out; no payment for a place that is not.

phrases.english: This one is where it stands to be rented out,
that one is where it does not stand to be rented out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ruling is about a different type of property
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rulings are about the same kind of property and so contradict
steps.terutzMaskana: The rent ruling is about property normally rented out; the no-rent ruling is about property that is not

steps.title: A reason from a פסוק: empty houses fall to ruin
steps.stepSummary: רב סחורה reports רב's ruling with a reason from a פסוק: an empty house gets ruined, so the person living there is helping the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סחורה said in the name of רב הונא, in the name of רב: someone who lives in his friend's courtyard without permission does not need to pay rent, because it says, 'and the gate is struck into ruin.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא gives a reason why no rent is owed. It quotes a פסוק saying that an empty house falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that the squatter is not hurting the owner at all. By living there, he keeps the house from becoming a ruin, so he is actually doing the owner a favor.

keyTerms.meaning: Because it is said: introducing a פסוק as the reason
Ruin or desolation that strikes an empty place
The gate is struck

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the reason behind the 'no rent' ruling. The squatter actually benefits the owner, so it is not just that the owner lost nothing.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב סְחוֹרָה אָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Sechora said that Rav Huna said that Rav said:
One who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge
does not need to pay him rent,
because it is said:
"And the gate is struck into ruin."
phrases.notes: ישעיה 24:12. The idea is that a house nobody lives in gets struck by ruin.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סְחוֹרָה אָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from settling the contradiction to explaining the reason for the no-rent ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No rent is owed, because living in an empty house protects it from ruin

steps.title: מר בר רב אשי saw how harmful it is
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי says he saw this ruin himself, and it strikes hard like a goring ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי said: I myself saw it, and it gores like an ox.
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי adds his own eyewitness account to show that the ruin from the פסוק is real and very damaging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He backs up רב's reason. The harm to an empty house is serious, so the person living there really is helping the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: I myself saw it
And it gores like an ox

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi said:
I myself saw it,
phrases.notes: "It" is the שְׁאִיָּה from the פסוק, the ruin that strikes empty houses.

phrases.english: and it gores like an ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי לְדִידִי חֲזֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the פסוק-based reason with an eyewitness report
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruin that strikes empty houses is real and very damaging

steps.title: רב יוסף: a lived-in house stays standing
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives a different reason: a house that people live in stays in good shape.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: a house that is lived in stays settled.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives his own reason why the squatter helps the owner. It is a plainer reason than the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב יוסף, the benefit is everyday upkeep. When someone lives in a house, it gets looked after and does not fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: A house that is lived in
Stays settled, stays standing in good shape

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
A house that is lived in stays settled.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר בֵּיתָא מְיַתְּבָא יָתֵיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second reason alongside רב's reason from the פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No rent is owed because living in a house keeps it maintained

steps.title: What is the difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רב's reason and רב יוסף's reason would lead to different results.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move by asking for a case where the two reasons would give different rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both reasons say the squatter helps the house. The גמרא wants to find a case where they actually disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two reasons just given
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where the two reasons lead to different rulings

steps.title: A house used for storing wood and straw
steps.stepSummary: The two reasons differ when the owner already uses the house to store wood and straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is where the owner uses the house for wood and straw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the case where the two reasons split: a house that is not empty but that nobody lives in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The storage use already keeps the house from being totally empty, so the ruin from the פסוק does not strike it. By that reason, the squatter adds nothing and would have to pay. By רב יוסף's reason, a person living there still keeps the house in better shape, so the squatter helps and pays nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
Wood, sticks
Straw

steps.whatToRemember: There are two reasons why a squatter does not pay rent: the פסוק about ruin, and רב יוסף's 'a lived-in house stays settled.' They differ for a house already used for storage.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
where he uses it for wood and straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the practical difference
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A house the owner uses for storing wood and straw: by the פסוק's reason the squatter adds nothing, while by רב יוסף's reason his living there still helps the house

steps.title: A man builds a mansion on the orphans' garbage heap
steps.stepSummary: A man built a mansion on a garbage heap that belonged to orphans, and רב נחמן took the mansion away from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who built a mansion on a garbage heap that belonged to orphans. רב נחמן took the mansion away from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about a ruling of רב נחמן. It is setting up the next move, where the גמרא will try to learn something from this story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land was not his. It belonged to orphans, and it was only a garbage heap. רב נחמן's harsh ruling, taking the whole building, looks like it could clash with רב's ruling that someone who lives in another's property without permission does not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: A mansion, a large and fancy building
A garbage heap or dump
Orphans
He took it away (confiscated it) from him

phrases.english: A certain man who built a mansion
on a garbage heap belonging to orphans.
Rav Nachman took his mansion away from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new story that may bear on the question of living in someone else's property without permission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן confiscated the mansion built on the orphans' garbage heap.

steps.title: Does this story prove a squatter must pay rent?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב נחמן holds that someone who lives on another's property without permission must pay rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רב נחמן holds that someone who lives in his friend's courtyard without the friend knowing has to pay him rent?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to use the story as proof for the big question: does a person who lives in another's property without permission have to pay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן punished the builder for using the orphans' land, and a garbage heap is not normally rented out. That looks like he thinks using someone's property creates a debt even when the owner loses nothing. If so, רב נחמן would disagree with the no-rent ruling reported in the name of רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It opens a suggested proof that may be rejected
One who lives in his friend's courtyard
Without his knowledge or permission
To pay him rent

phrases.english: Shall we say that Rav Nachman holds:
one who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge
must pay him rent?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a proposed legal conclusion from the story in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That one who lives in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב נחמן's confiscation of the mansion built on the orphans' land.

steps.title: No proof: the orphans actually lost money
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. Carmanians used to pay the orphans a little for the land, and the builder ignored רב נחמן's order to make it up to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: That case was different. At first Carmanians lived on that land and gave the orphans a small payment. רב נחמן told the man: Go make peace with the orphans. He ignored it, so רב נחמן took the mansion from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the proof. The story was a special case where the owners really lost income.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our question is about an owner who loses nothing. Here the orphans lost a small income because the Carmanians were no longer there, and the man also refused רב נחמן's order. So the confiscation was a penalty for real loss and defiance, and it proves nothing about a squatter who causes no loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Originally, at first
Carmanians, a wandering people who camped there
A small amount
Appease them, make it up to them
And he paid no attention

steps.confusionAlert: Don't take this story as proof that every squatter pays rent. רב נחמן ruled this way only because the orphans lost real money and the man refused to fix it.

phrases.english: That case is different: originally
Carmanians used to live on it,
and they would give the orphans a small amount.
He said to him: Go and appease the orphans,
phrases.notes: רב נחמן is telling the builder to make up the orphans' lost income.

phrases.english: but he paid no attention.
So Rav Nachman took his mansion away from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא – מֵעִיקָּרָא קַרְמְנָאֵי הֲווֹ דָּיְירִי בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 19 by showing the case involved real loss.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference that רב נחמן makes a squatter pay rent. The no-rent ruling for property that is not normally rented out still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The story involved real lost income and defiance of the court, not a case where the owner loses nothing.
steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן's story proves nothing about the squatter question, because the orphans lost income and the builder ignored the court.

steps.title: רב and שמואל on an animal that turns its head to eat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about paying for benefit. רב says 'pays for the damage' applies when the animal turns its head to the side of the square; שמואל says even then the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: How does it pay for what it benefited, etc. רב said: This is even when the animal stands in the square and turns its head to the side. שמואל said: Even when it turns its head, the owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: a line from the משנה about an animal that eats food in the public square. רב and שמואל argue about one case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that if the animal eats from the side of the square, the owner pays the full damage. רב reads that as an animal standing in the public area that only stretches its head over to the side. שמואל says that if the animal itself is in the public area, the owner is exempt even when it turns its head.

keyTerms.meaning: How? It opens the משנה's explanation
What it benefited, the value of the food it enjoyed
Turns, the animal turns its head to the side
Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: "How does it pay for what it benefited, etc."
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The part that matters is its next line: eating at the side of the square means paying full damage.

phrases.english: Rav said: and this is when it turns its head.
phrases.notes: רב means the animal's body is in the public square and only its head reaches the food at the side.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
Even when it turns its head, he is also exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the squatter topic and returns to explaining the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: an animal that turns its head to the side of the square makes its owner pay full damage. שמואל: in that case the owner is exempt.

steps.title: How does שמואל explain the משנה's liability?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks שמואל: if turning the head is exempt, when is the owner liable as the משנה says?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to שמואל, how can you find a case where the owner is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל. His view seems to leave the משנה's ruling of liability with no case to apply to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה clearly says that eating at the side of the square makes the owner pay for the damage. If שמואל exempts the head-turning case, the גמרא wants to know what case the משנה is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you find it? Show me the case
That he is liable

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel,
how can you find a case where he is liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's position from step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's exemption for an animal that turns its head.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה rules liability for eating at the side of the square, so שמואל must still have some case where that applies.

steps.title: The animal walked over and stood at the side
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's case of liability: the animal left the open square and actually stood at the side where the food was.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, when the animal left the square and went and stood at the side of the square.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for שמואל by giving a case where the owner is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, what matters is where the animal's body stands. If the whole animal moves to the side of the square, which is not public walking space, it is like eating in the damaged person's own property, so the animal's owner pays full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, such as
The open square, public space
The sides of the square, not a public walkway

phrases.english: For example, where it left the square,
and went and stood at the sides of the square.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a narrower case for the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל seemed to leave the משנה's liability with no case.
steps.terutzMaskana: For שמואל, the משנה means the animal itself stood at the side of the square.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: turning the head to the side means liable. שמואל: only an animal that actually stands at the side makes its owner liable.

steps.title: Second version: the argument as a stand-alone dispute
steps.stepSummary: Some teach the רב/שמואל argument on its own, not as an explanation of the משנה: if the animal turns its head, רב says liable and שמואל says exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some teach this teaching on its own: an animal that turns its head. רב said it is liable, and שמואל said it is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way the same argument was passed down, as a separate dispute instead of a comment on the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rulings are the same as before. What changes is the frame: here רב and שמואל argue directly about the head-turning case, without attaching it to the משנה's words.

keyTerms.meaning: And there are those who teach it differently
A teaching or ruling
On its own, independently
Liable, has to pay

phrases.english: And there are those who teach this teaching
on its own:
phrases.notes: He means as a separate argument, not as an explanation of the משנה's words.

phrases.english: An animal that turns its head: Rav said: it is liable,
and Shmuel said: it is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּאַפֵּי נַפְשָׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates the step 21 dispute in a different frame.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Head-turning case: רב says liable, שמואל says exempt.

steps.title: Second version: the same challenge to שמואל
steps.stepSummary: Even in this version the גמרא asks how שמואל can explain the משנה's words 'it pays for what it damaged.'
steps.simpleTranslation: According to שמואל, the משנה says 'it pays for what it damaged.' How can you find a case where it is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל again, this time quoting the משנה's exact words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the argument started on its own, the משנה still rules liability for eating at the side of the square. So שמואל needs a case where that applies.

keyTerms.meaning: It pays for what it damaged, full damage

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel,
"it pays for what it damaged"
how can you find a case where it is liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִשְׁמוּאֵל מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁהִזִּיקָה הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ דִּמְחַיְּיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל within the second version.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's exemption in the stand-alone version.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה rules full damage for eating at the side, so שמואל must have a case where that applies.

steps.title: Second version: same answer, the animal stood at the side
steps.stepSummary: The answer is the same: the animal left the square and stood at the side of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, when the animal left the square and went and stood at the side of the square.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the same way as before. In this version too, שמואל's case of liability is an animal standing at the side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions agree on how שמואל reads the משנה. Liability comes only when the animal's body is in the non-public side area. The two versions differ only in how the argument is framed.

keyTerms.meaning: And it stood

phrases.english: For example, where it left the square,
and went and stood at the sides of the square.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25 with the same case as step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a narrower case for the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל seemed to leave no case for the משנה's liability.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה's liability is for an animal that physically stands at the side of the square.
steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, רב makes the owner pay when the animal only turns its head, and שמואל makes him pay only when the animal actually stands at the side of the square.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from the store entrance case
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק argues that the משנה's store-entrance case must involve an animal turning its head. Yet the owner only pays for the benefit, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק objects: The משנה says that if the animal ate from the entrance of a store, the owner pays only for what it benefited. How could that happen? Obviously the animal turned its head to reach the store. And still the משנה says 'what it benefited.' So he pays for the benefit, yes, but not for the full damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a challenge against רב, who said an owner is liable for full damage when his animal turns its head to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal walking in the street can only reach the store's entrance by turning its head. If רב were right, the owner should pay full damages. But the משנה says he pays only for the benefit the animal got, which sounds like שמואל's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from a משנה or ברייתא
The entrance of a store, which counts like the public area
The animal turns its head to the side
What it benefited: the owner pays only the value the animal enjoyed
What it damaged: the owner pays the full damage

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak raises an objection:
If it ate from the entrance of the store, it pays what it benefited.
How can you find this case?
Obviously, where it turns its head;
and he (the Master) says 'what it benefited',
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't. Either way, it means the משנה says this.

phrases.english: what it benefited, yes,
what it damaged, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רב's side of the argument (turning the head makes the owner liable) and attacks it from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that an animal turning its head makes its owner liable for full damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eating from a store entrance must involve turning the head. Yet the משנה requires only payment for benefit, so turning the head must not create full liability.

steps.title: The store is on a corner
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers his own challenge. The store is at a corner, so the produce lay right in the animal's path and it never turned its head.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised the question and he answered it: the case is where the store stands at a corner.
steps.whatsHappening: The same רב נחמן בר יצחק who asked the question now answers it, and saves רב's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At a corner, the store's produce sits right where the animal is walking as it rounds the turn. So the animal ate without turning its head at all. That is why the owner pays only for the benefit, and רב's rule still stands.

keyTerms.term: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ
keyTerms.meaning: He asked it and he answered it: the same person raises the question and resolves it
A corner

phrases.aramaic: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ:
phrases.english: He raised the objection and he resolved it:
where it stands at a corner.
phrases.notes: He means the store sits at a corner, so the food is right in the animal's way.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the משנה is placed in a specific setup where no head-turning happens.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed eating from a store entrance always requires turning the head.
steps.terutzMaskana: At a corner store the produce is directly in the animal's path, so paying only for benefit fits with רב.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's rule survives: the store-entrance case is a corner store, where the animal never turned its head.

steps.title: Another version: the argument is about space given to the public
steps.stepSummary: A second version says everyone agrees turning the head makes the owner liable. רב and שמואל really argue about space a person sets aside from his property for public use.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: When the animal turns its head, everyone agrees the owner is liable. Where they disagree is when a person sets aside space from his own property and adds it to the public area.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a completely different version of what רב and שמואל argue about. This line sets up their actual statements, which come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, head-turning is no longer the argument at all; both agree it makes the owner liable. The new question is about a strip of private land left open for the public to use. Does damage there count as happening in a private area or in the public area?

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say: introduces another version
Everyone agrees
Sets aside space
The public domain

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In the first version they argue about turning the head. In this version they both agree on that, and they argue only about space set aside for the public.

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: מַחְזֶרֶת – כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּחַיֶּיבֶת.
phrases.english: Where it turns its head, everyone agrees that it is liable.
Where they disagree
is where one sets aside space from his property for the public domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the earlier ways of explaining the רב/שמואל argument with a new topic for their dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Turning the head makes the owner liable according to everyone. The dispute is only about private space set aside for public use.

steps.title: רב and שמואל on space set aside for the public
steps.stepSummary: רב says the משנה's liability applies only to head-turning, and the owner is exempt in set-aside space. שמואל says the owner is liable even there.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is how it was stated: רב said, the משנה taught liability only when the animal turns its head. But if a person set aside space from his property for the public, the owner of the animal is exempt. שמואל said: even if he set aside space from his property for the public, the owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the actual words of רב and שמואל in this second version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats the set-aside strip as part of the public area, so the animal's owner is exempt there. שמואל treats it as still private property, so the animal's owner is liable even there.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught: limits a teaching to a specific case
His own property
Exempt
Liable

steps.whatToRemember: Second version: everyone holds head-turning is liable. On set-aside space, רב says exempt and שמואל says liable.

phrases.english: And this is how it was stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא מַחְזֶרֶת,
phrases.english: Rav said: They taught liability only where it turns its head,
but if one sets aside space from his property
for the public domain, it is exempt.
And Shmuel said:
Even if one sets aside space from his property
for the public domain, it is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָכִי אִתְּמַר, אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא מַחְזֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the actual statements that step 29 introduced.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: exempt in space set aside for the public. שמואל: liable even there.

steps.title: Suggesting the argument depends on a pit dug in one's own property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב and שמואל's argument about set-aside space is really the known argument about a בור dug in one's own property and later given up. רב, who exempts the animal's owner, would hold the pit-digger liable. שמואל, who makes the animal's owner liable, would hold the pit-digger exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about a pit in one's own property? רב, who says the animal's owner is exempt, holds that one who digs a pit in his own property is liable. שמואל, who says the animal's owner is liable, holds that one who digs a pit in his own property is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is testing a theory: maybe רב and שמואל's argument is really a known argument about a בור dug in one's own property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a person digs a pit on his land and then gives up the land (but not the pit), is the pit treated as if it is in public space? If yes (liable), then set-aside space also counts as public, so the animal's owner is exempt, like רב. If no (exempt), the space still counts as the owner's own, so the animal's owner is liable, like שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It opens a suggestion that the גמרא will test.
A pit dug inside one's own property
They disagree
He holds, meaning this is his underlying view

phrases.english: Shall we say they disagree about a pit in one's own property?
phrases.notes: Someone dug a pit on his own land and later gave up the land, but not the pit.

phrases.english: Rav, who says the owner is exempt,
holds: one who digs a pit in his own property is liable.
And Shmuel, who says the owner is liable,
holds: one who digs a pit in his own property is exempt?

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the flip. רב says 'exempt' about the animal but 'liable' about the pit. Both come from one idea: the given-up space counts as public.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the second version of the argument from steps 29-30 and tries to connect it to a known argument about a pit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the argument between רב and שמואל about set-aside space simply match the argument about a בור dug in one's own property?

steps.title: רב begins to reject the suggested link
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to push back on the suggestion, saying רב could answer that the two arguments are not linked. The full answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב could say to you: Actually, I will tell you:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is starting to reject the suggestion, and רב's actual explanation comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'Actually, I will tell you' tells us רב will explain his view another way. He wants to show that his ruling does not force him to take a side on the pit argument.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you. It introduces how a sage would defend himself.
Actually, really. It signals a defense of the original position.
I will tell you

phrases.english: Rav could say to you:
Actually, I will tell you:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב, לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins rejecting the link suggested in step 31.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that רב's ruling forces him into one side of the pit argument.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Not yet stated. רב's explanation follows in the next lines.
